# Page 7^page=7
Definition: Tensor De˝nition In orthogonal coordinate system , a quantity is a tensor if each of the free su˚ces transform in a certain way under rotation of the coordinates. For instance, Rank 2: T ′ ij = LimLjnTmn, Rank 3: T ′ ijk = LimLjnLkpTmnp, Rank 4: T ′ ijkℓ = LimLjnLkpLℓqTmnpq, etc. Note that on the RHS m, n, p and q are repeated dummy indices (summed over), and i, j, k, and ℓ are free indices. Thus, the equation balances. 4 24

# Page 8^page=8
Definition: Rank De˝nition The rank or order of a tensor is the number of free indices. Example A 3 × 3 matrix M is written as Mij with two free indices i and j which act as row and column counters. Thus, Mij is a second-rank tensor. Remark A tensor may have any number of free indices. For instance, a rank 7 tensor Pijkℓmnp transforms via: P ′ ijkℓmnp = LiaLjbLkcLℓdLmeLnf LpgPabcdef g. 5 24

# Page 9^page=9
Example 1: Kronecker Delta Example 1: Kronecker Delta The Kronecker Delta δij is a second-rank tensor. To show this, we must show δ′ ij = LikLjmδkm. In fact, recall that LikLjk = δij. Thus, LikLjmδkm = LikLjk = δij. Since δij is de˝ned in the same in any coordinate system, δij = δ′ ij. Thus, LikLjmδkm = δ′ ij. 6 24

# Page 10^page=10
Example 2: The Gradient of a Vector Example 2: The Gradient of a Vector Show that ∇u = ∂ui ∂xj is a second-rank tensor. We must show ∂u′ i ∂x′ j = LikLjℓ ∂uk ∂xℓ . Recall that u ′ i = Likuk and ∂xi ∂x′ j = Lji. Thus, ∂u′ i ∂x′ j = ∂Likuk ∂x′ j = Lik ∂uk ∂x′ j + uk ∂Lik ∂x′ j ︸ ︷︷ ︸ product rule . 7 24

# Page 11^page=11
Remark Remark Recall that ∂x′ i ∂xk = Lik and ∂xi ∂x′ k = Lki. Thus, ∂Lik ∂x′ j = ∂ ∂x′ j ( ∂x′ i ∂xk ) = ∂2x′ i ∂x′ j∂xk = ∂2x′ i ∂xk∂x′ j = ∂ ∂xk ( ∂x′ i ∂x′ j ) = ∂ ∂xk (δij) = 0. . 8 24

# Page 12^page=12
Example 2: The Gradient of a Vector Example 2: The Gradient of a Vector Show that ∇u = ∂ui ∂xj is a second-rank tensor. We must show ∂u′ i ∂x′ j = LikLjℓ ∂uk ∂xℓ . So far, we have ∂u′ i ∂x′ j = Lik ∂uk ∂x′ j + uk ∂Lik ∂x′ j ︸ ︷︷ ︸ = 0 = Lik ∂uk ∂x′ j = Lik ∂uk ∂xℓ ∂xℓ ∂x′ j ︸ ︷︷ ︸ chain rule = Lik ∂uk ∂xℓ Ljℓ ︸ ︷︷ ︸ ∂xℓ ∂x′ j =Ljℓ = LikLjℓ ∂uk ∂xℓ . 9 24

# Page 14^page=14
The quotient rule

# Page 15^page=15
The quotient rule Lemma (The quotient rule) Suppose there is a quantity Tij such that in all rotated coordinate systems , we have that for any vector b, Tijbj is a vector. In other words, the resulting quantity a given by ai = Tijbj is a vector. Then Tij is a tensor. 11 24

# Page 16^page=16
Proof: The quotient rule Proof. Assumptions: A1. b is a vector i.e. b′ m = Lmjbj or bj = Lmjb′ m, A2. We can write ak = Tkjbj, A3. a is a vector i.e. a′ i = Likak. We want to show: Tij is a tensor i.e. T ′ ij = LikLjmTkm. 12 24

# Page 17^page=17
Proof: The quotient rule Proof. Assumptions: A1. b is a vector i.e. b′ m = Lmjbj or bj = Lmjb′ m, A2. We can write ak = Tkjbj, A3. a is a vector i.e. a′ i = Likak. On the one hand, a ′ i = Likak = LikTkjbj (A3 & A2) = LikTkjLmjb ′ m (A1) = LikLmjTkjb ′ m. On the other hand, a ′ i = T ′ imb ′ m. (A2 holds in all coordinate systems) 13 24

# Page 18^page=18
Proof: The quotient rule Proof. Thus, we conclude 0 = a′ i − a′ i = T ′ imb ′ m − LikLmjTkjb ′ m = (T ′ im − LikLmjTkj)b ′ m. Because b can be any vector, we can assume b′ m ̸= 0. We then obtain T ′ im − LikLmjTkj = 0. That is, T ′ im = LikLmjTkj. Therefore, Tij is a second-rank tensor. 14 24

# Page 19^page=19
Symmetric and Antisymmet- ric Tensors

# Page 20^page=20
Definition: Symmetric and antisymmetric tensors De˝nition. A second-rank tensor Tij is symmetric if Tij = Tji. De˝nition. A second-rank tensor Tij is antisymmetric if Tij = −Tji. Example. We know that the Kronecker delta is symmetric: δij = δji. 15 24

# Page 21^page=21
Definition: Symmetric and antisymmetric tensors - higher rank De˝nition. A tensor of rank greater than two can be symmetric or antisymmetric with respect to any pair of indices . Example. The alternating tensor ϵijk is antisymmetric: ϵijk = −ϵjik, ϵijk = −ϵikj, and ϵijk = −ϵkji. 16 24

# Page 22^page=22
Symmetry Lemma Lemma. Symmetry is a physical property of tensors. In other words, if a tensor is symmetric in a Cartesian coordinate system then it is also symmetric in any other Cartesian coordinate systems. Proof. Proof Suppose that Aij is a symmetric tensor. That is, Aij = Aji. Then in a rotated frame, we have A′ ij = LikLjmAkm = LikLjm Amk︸︷︷︸ symmetric = LjmLik ︸ ︷︷ ︸ re-order Amk = A′ ji. Thus, A′ ij is also symmetric. 17 24

# Page 23^page=23
Example 1 Example 1 Show that any second-rank tensor Tij can be written as the sum of a symmetric tensor and an antisymmetric tensor. For any tensor Tij, Tij + Tji is symmetric, Tij − Tji is antisymmetric. We write Tij using sums of these symmetric and anti-symmetric tensors: Tik = 1 2 (Tik + Tki) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ Sik + 1 2 (Tik − Tki) ︸ ︷︷ ︸ Aik . Thus, Tik = Sik + Aik. 18 24

# Page 24^page=24
Remark: Symmetrisation Symmetrisation Notation: Sik = 1 2 (Tik + Tki) is called the symmetric part of Tik, Aik = 1 2 (Tik − Tki) is called the antisymmetric part of Tik Moreover, Constructing Sik from an arbitrary tensor with components Tik is called symmetrisation , Constructing Aik from an arbitrary tensor with components Tik is called antisymmetrisation . 19 24

# Page 25^page=25
Example 2 Example 2 A second-rank tensor Tij obeys ϵijkTjk = 0i. Show that Tij is a symmetric tensor. Recall the alternating tensor ϵijk =    0 if any of i, j, k are equal , +1 if (i, j, k) = (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 1) or (3, 1, 2), −1 if (i, j, k) = (1, 3, 2), (2, 1, 3) or (3, 2, 1). Taking i = 1, we obtain ϵ1jkTjk = ∑ j ∑ k ϵ1jkTjk = ϵ123T23 + ϵ132T32︸ ︷︷ ︸ only non-zero components = T23 − T32. 20 24

# Page 26^page=26
Example 2 - Part 2 Example 2 A second-rank tensor Tij obeys ϵijkTjk = 0i. Show that Tij is a symmetric tensor. Now, because ϵijkTjk = 0i, and ϵijkTjk = T23 − T32, we see that T23 = T32. If we repeat this for i = 2 and i = 3, we get T12 = T21 and T13 = T31. We then conclude that Tij = Tji, hence Tij is symmetric. 21 24
